extracted.intended_audience: readers of Darwin's correspondence; historians of science; scholars of 19th-century natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction and interpretation of evaluative principles, methodological notes, and ethical judgments embedded in Charles Darwin's letters (mid-19th century). Useful for editors, historians, or researchers annotating scientific correspondence for methodological and ethical guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medal-awarding principle: favour early-career recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: More good is done by giving medals to younger men in the early part of their career than as a mere reward to men whose scientific career is nearly finished; perhaps medals could be better applied EXCLUSIVELY to such men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin argues he is 'almost inclined to think that I would rather lower the standard, and give medals to young workers than to old ones with no ESPECIAL claims.' He warns that admitting general claims opens the door to laxity; 'especial claims which can be put down on paper' are preferable. He questions whether wealthy patrons who aided only with money should receive medals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer documented 'especial claims' for awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards/medals should ideally be tied to 'especial claims' that can be 'put down on paper' rather than vague or general justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin notes that if 'general claims are once admitted, it opens the door to great laxity in giving them,' and thus favors specificity and written documentation of the claim when considering awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/priority ethics when receiving unsolicited ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When a third party sends an outline of ideas (e.g., Wallace's sketch), one must consider whether using that stimulus to publish would be 'dishonourable' or unfairly take advantage of the other's unsolicited communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin reflects on whether publishing a sketch of his views after Wallace sent his outline would be 'base and paltry' and worries that being induced to publish by having privately known Wallace was 'hard on me' but may not alter the justice of the case. He and his correspondents consider joint presentation and disclosure of prior sketches as remedies; the interest of science generally may also justify actions (as per Lyell/Hooker's intervention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit and transparency in claims of priority
rubrics_metrics.description: When circumstances of overlapping discovery arise, disclose prior manuscripts/copies and correspondences to demonstrate independent development and to avoid unjustly taking credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin offers to show his 1844 sketch and a short earlier letter to Asa Gray to prove he took 'nothing from Wallace.' He supports communicating openly with peers (Lyell, Hooker) and considering the interests of science generally in arranging publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of speculation to guide observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Speculation is necessary: 'without speculation there is no good and original observation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin explicitly states that he is 'a firm believer that without speculation there is no good and original observation,' and praises Wallace for 'attending to distribution in accordance with theoretical ideas.' This is presented as methodological guidance: theory (speculation) and observation inform each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine multiple independent lines of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Integrate geological and biological evidence (e.g., coral-reef and glacial data) when addressing distribution and modification of species to strengthen inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin cites combining evidence from coral reefs and erratic boulders/glacial action with biological distribution and modification as throwing 'a flood of light on the whole subject of distribution.' He uses cross-disciplinary evidence to argue for broader conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware recording bias in Floras when studying varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: When using floras or prodromuses to study the frequency of varieties, consider whether botanists unconsciously record varieties more (or less) in large genera than in small genera — i.e., account for recorder bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin repeatedly asks correspondents whether 'good botanists ... would almost universally, but unintentionally and unconsciously, tend to record ... varieties in the large or in the small genera?' He warns that his conclusions must allow for 'many causes of error' and that the question is specifically about tendency to RECORD varieties, not raw frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for testing the 'varieties in large genera' hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabulate species by genus size and compare proportions of species presenting marked varieties to test whether larger genera have more recorded varieties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin describes dividing the New Zealand flora as suggested (e.g., species in genera of 4 and upwards vs. genera of 3 and less) and computing proportions (e.g., 339 species had 51 showing varieties; 323 species had 37). He stresses that such tabulation is 'hard work' but an appropriate way to test the hypothesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude universally variable parts when assessing abnormal development
rubrics_metrics.description: When testing whether abnormal developments (or Waterhouse's law) are correlated with high variability of an organ, consider excluding parts that are highly variable across all species of a group (possible polymorphism) to avoid confounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin suggests 'PERHAPS cases in which a part is highly variable in all the species of a group should be excluded, as possibly being something distinct, and connected with the perplexing subject of polymorphism.' He worries that measuring slight variations is difficult and that some plant parts show general variability making comparison hard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical, open-eyed observation and collecting parallel cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep eyes open to natural occurrences (e.g., stripes in horses, wing bars in pigeons), collect parallel facts across breeds/species, and use these parallels to infer ancestral conditions or causal hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin asks correspondents to note occurrences of spinal bands, leg bars, and shoulder-stripes in various horse breeds, to record parallels in crossed animals, and to relate such observations to possible ancestral colouring. He frames this as small, cumulative observational evidence that could 'throw light on the colour of the primeval horse.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Select well-worked floras with varieties marked for comparative studies
rubrics_metrics.description: When searching literature for data on varieties, prioritize well-worked regional floras/prodromuses (1,000–2,000 species) that mark varieties, since these are more useful for tabulation and comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Darwin requests suggestions of 'well-worked Floras with from 1000-2000 species, with the varieties marked' and lists specific works/authors he has used. He explicitly seeks floras where varieties are indicated (e.g., by Greek letters) to enable reliable tabulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution on highly prejudiced topics (e.g., 'man')
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid tackling socially charged or prejudiced topics lightly; be aware that some subjects (Darwin mentions 'man') are surrounded by prejudices that may impair objective treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discussing 'man' due to surrounding prejudices
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid treating highly prejudiced topics (e.g., human evolution) in a way that invites misinterpretation; Darwin prefers to 'avoid the whole subject' of man as it is 'so surrounded with prejudices.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He acknowledges that though the topic is 'the highest and most interesting problem for the naturalist,' the prejudices make objective treatment difficult and so he may refrain from including it in his work.
